Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration : https://t.co/Cfj54yOqsg

"Deepthika SDepartment of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Amrita School of Engineering, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore, 641112, IndiaPawni YadavNew Delhi, 110078, IndiaB. Sankarsankarb@iisc.ac.inCorresponding author. Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, 560012, India
Abstract
Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant’s briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modelled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human–AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

1Introduction
For a species as social as ours, survival has never depended on the individual alone. In evolutionary biology, fitness describes an organism’s capacity to survive and reproduce in its environment; for humans, that capacity has been shaped by life in groups, where cooperation, communication and resource sharing are routine. The cognitive demands of such relationships are reflected in the unusually large primate neocortex, which has been linked to the need to track relationships within social groups (Dunbar, 1992). Food sharing illustrates the point. In many hunter-gatherer societies a successful hunt feeds more than the hunter: large, unpredictably acquired food packages tend to be widely distributed, partly because the cost of not sharing outweighs the benefit of eating alone (Hawkes et al., 2018). With repeated interaction, sharing and reciprocity become patterned, particularly where camp membership is stable (Smith et al., 2016). Cooperation among kin is explained by inclusive fitness (Hamilton, 1964), whereas cooperation among non-kin rests partly on the expectation that partners will reciprocate (Rand and Nowak, 2013). Repeated cooperation therefore produces more than an exchange of resources. It produces expectations about how others will behave, and those expectations are a basis for https://t.co/wRHNabWgPY societies grew more complex, so did the relationships through which such expectations form. Human social networks are layered, from an intimate core of family and close friends to acquaintances at the margins, and the layers differ in contact frequency, emotional closeness, reciprocity and trust (Dunbar, 2025). Nor is trust static within a relationship. It starts from some baseline and moves as experience accumulates: perceptions of predictability grow from observing the consistency of a partner’s behaviour (Camanto and Campbell, 2025), and trust strengthens when positive expectations are confirmed and weakens when they are violated (Lewicki et al., 2006). Trust is less a fixed property of a relationship than a running account of expectation and outcome, and the degree to which A trusts B need not equal the degree to which B trusts https://t.co/o229aVXh3c a relationship even necessary? Not always. A patient trusts a doctor they have never met, and a passenger trusts a pilot they will never see. Non-experts routinely rely on expert knowledge they cannot verify, such as a physician’s diagnosis (Leefmann and Lesle, 2020). Such trust rests on competence, professional standards, reputation and institutions rather than on familiarity: “swift trust” forms among strangers through recognisable roles, and trust in a stockbroker is bounded by regulation rather than by acquaintance (Lewicki et al., 2006). A relationship is one basis for trust, not a prerequisite for it.Yet the trust we extend to strangers is usually cautious. We hesitate before trusting someone we have never met, not because they are untrustworthy but because we lack information about them: their history, their intentions, the relationship between us. Seen this way, an AI assistant is an extreme case. It has no personal history, no body, no reputation built through shared experience and no intentions we can read, and it is not even a stranger in the usual sense, because a stranger is at least another person. If people are wary of trusting a human being they do not know, why would they trust something that is not human at all? One answer is that such trust does not need a relationship, because it can rest instead on the kind of reliability we attribute to machines.We expect a calculator to return 4 for 2+2, an ATM to dispense the right amount and a lift to stop at the chosen floor. Trust in such systems tracks the reliability of their performance and the extent to which that performance meets expectations (McKenna et al., 2024); consistent performance reinforces trust and failures undermine it (Parasuraman and Riley, 1997; de Visser et al., 2018). Crucially, expectation and outcome can be compared. The function is defined, the output is verifiable, and reliability is observable across repeated use. Where expectation and outcome overlap, reliability is established; reliability confirmed over repeated trials becomes confidence; and confidence becomes trust (Figure 1, top).Conversational AI breaks this arrangement (Figure 1, bottom). Large language models have moved human–computer interaction from specialised, task-bound automation towards systems that act as advisers (Henrique and Santos, 2024; Klingbeil et al., 2024). People ask them “What should I do?”, “Which option is better?” and “Can you explain this to me?”, questions without a single predetermined answer against which a response can be checked. An AI system can also be wrong while sounding coherent and certain. With a calculator, the user checks whether a function was performed correctly; with AI, the user must judge whether the information itself is accurate enough to rely on, often on a topic they are trying to learn precisely because they do not know it. Reliance on such systems is already known to be unstable: people sometimes discount good computerised advice (Promberger and Baron, 2006) and, in other conditions, follow AI advice against contrary evidence and their own judgement (Klingbeil et al., 2024). And if trust is built through repeated experiences of something meeting our expectations, a system that is trained to meet expectations—to sound right, to agree, to please—can meet them while being wrong.📷Figure 1:The calculator fallacy. Top: trust in a deterministic tool is earned through verification, because the user can compare output with expectation and accumulate evidence of reliability. Bottom: with conversational AI, the learner cannot verify, fluency and confidence stand in for reliability, and “checking” routes back to the same source, closing a loop in which trust cannot calibrate.
This creates an under-studied failure mode at the intersection of two literatures. Research on trust in automation asks whether people’s trust tracks a system’s reliability (Lee and See, 2004; Hoff and Bashir, 2015). Research on sycophancy asks whether LLMs tailor their answers to what users want rather than to what is true (Perez et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2024). Both typically treat one side of the human–AI pair as fixed. Sycophancy research, in particular, measures whether the model adapts to the user: whether it abandons a correct answer under pushback, mirrors a stated opinion or flatters the user’s self-image (Fanous et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026). The reverse direction has received far less attention: when the model holds its ground confidently and consistently, does the user adapt to the model? We call this human-side deference: the convergence of a person’s beliefs on a source’s claims irrespective of their truth. It is the mirror image of model sycophancy, and it matters because modern assistants are, by design, fluent, assertive and unhedged (Zhou et al., 2024).We report HARICHAN (Human–AI Reliance in CHAt iNteractions), a controlled experiment in which the same LLM taught five science topics while covertly falsifying between none and all of its briefing facts, always with full confidence. We address five research questions:
https://t.co/T6Gx9jWtYq much planted misinformation do learners absorb as falsification rises, and does their acceptance of each stated falsehood change with the source’s overall reliability?
RQ2.Does learners’ confidence distinguish what they learned correctly from what they absorbed falsely?
RQ3.Does their reported trust track the assistant’s actual reliability?
https://t.co/T6BZg7yEgQ do learners check an assistant they have reason to doubt, and what happens when they push back?
https://t.co/SIzfvWtu2g the deference sycophancy on the model’s side or on the human’s, and how does human-side deference relate to confidence?Our contributions are fourfold. Empirically, we measure misinformation uptake across a graded range of assistant reliability in open-ended conversational learning, and we separate exposure to a falsehood from acceptance of it by coding every transcript for which facts the assistant actually stated. Methodologically, we adapt baseline-corrected sycophancy metrics from model evaluation to the human side, introducing a Human Deference Index and pairing it with metacognitive measures of confidence. Conceptually, we argue that the “calculator fallacy”—extending to a fluent, probabilistic system the trust that deterministic tools earn through verification—explains why trust cannot calibrate when error is invisible, and that trustworthiness is a property of the human–AI pair. For design, we derive strategies that make reliability legible per claim, route verification outward and evaluate trust behaviourally.
2Related work

2.1Trust, reliance and calibration
Trust in automation is commonly defined as the attitude that an agent will help achieve one’s goals in a situation characterised by uncertainty and vulnerability (Lee and See, 2004), and in interpersonal terms as a willingness to be vulnerable that rests on perceived ability, benevolence and integrity (Mayer et al., 1995). The design goal is not more trust but calibrated trust: trust that matches a system’s actual capability (Lee and See, 2004; Wischnewski et al., 2023), or, in the terms of Jacovi et al. (2021), warranted rather than unwarranted trust. Lee and See (2004) also describe resolution, the degree to which changes in capability are mirrored by changes in trust, and specificity, the degree to which trust attaches to particular functions rather than to the system as a whole. Reviews of trust measurement emphasise that trust is latent and multifaceted, that most scales are bespoke, and that behavioural measures should accompany self-report (Gebru et al., 2022; Wischnewski et al., 2023). Trust and distrust also appear to be distinct factors rather than two ends of one scale (Scharowski et al., 2025), and healthy distrust may require both explicit error detection and an intuitive sense of when to doubt (Peters et al., 2026).Hoff and Bashir (2015) separate dispositional, situational and learned trust and note that learned trust updates dynamically with reliability, but only when people can compare the system’s performance with their own. Experiments bear this out. Stated and observed accuracy both shape trust, but observed accuracy dominates once users can see it (Yin et al., 2019); trust can drift away from reliability when no feedback is available (Rittenberg et al., 2024); and displaying an AI’s case-level confidence helps calibrate trust where explanations do not (Zhang et al., 2020). Computational models describe trust as moving towards recent experience, cumulative trust and a prior expectation bias; without outcome feedback, the experience term cannot register failure (Hu et al., 2019). For virtual and embedded AI, high initial trust typically drops after errors are experienced (Glikson and Woolley, 2020), and trust has affective as well as cognitive roots (Gillath et al., 2021; Choung et al., 2023). The recurring condition across this literature is visibility: trust calibrates to what users can observe.
2.2Overreliance and automation bias with conversational AI
When verification is costly, people lean on automated aids. Automation bias, the use of automated output as a substitute for vigilant information seeking, produces commission errors even when contradictory cues are available (Skitka et al., 1999; Goddard et al., 2012), and it shares an attentional mechanism with complacency that affects experts and novices alike (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010). Labelling advice as algorithmic increases its weight regardless of its quality (Logg et al., 2019), and AI-labelled advice can override both contextual evidence and people’s own assessments, at real cost (Klingbeil et al., 2024). Appropriate reliance requires both relying on correct advice and overriding incorrect advice (Schemmer et al., 2023); explanations can reduce overreliance when they lower the cost of verification (Vasconcelos et al., 2023) but can also inflate reliance when they merely justify (Dzindolet et al., 2003). Sundar (2020) attributes part of this to a “machine heuristic”, the lay belief that machines are objective and accurate, which invites users to outsource vigilance.Large language models intensify the problem because they are fluent by default and rarely express uncertainty; users rely on their confident outputs whether or not those outputs are correct (Zhou et al., 2024), and overreliance on overconfident models appears across languages (Rathi et al., 2025). Users overestimate the accuracy of model answers from default explanations, and longer explanations raise confidence without improving discrimination (Steyvers et al., 2025). Model-generated explanations speed up fact-checking but mislead when the model is convincingly wrong (Si et al., 2024); users overlooked the errors in ChatGPT answers to programming questions 39% of the time even though 52% of those answers were incorrect (Kabir et al., 2024); and LLM-based search is fast but invites overreliance when the model errs (Spatharioti et al., 2025). First-person hedging reduces overreliance only in part (Kim et al., 2024), sources and visible inconsistencies help more than explanations (Kim et al., 2025), and combining visual and verbal uncertainty cues can sharpen subjective discrimination while worsening behavioural reliance (Ojewale et al., 2026). In conversational settings, dialogue cues increase trust even when an assistant spreads health misinformation, and only acted-upon, independent verification lowers it (Liao and Sundar, 2026). AI assistance can also make people perform better while making them worse at judging their own performance (Fernandes et al., 2026), and human confidence in themselves, rather than in the AI, often governs whether advice is adopted (Chong et al., 2022). Most of this work, however, studies single decisions with a fixed error rate. Less is known about learning from a conversational source whose reliability varies, where the learner has no independent knowledge and the only readily available check is the source itself.
2.3Misinformation, fluency and epistemic vigilance
Research on misinformation explains why confidently stated falsehoods persist. Once encoded, misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after it is retracted, and corrections work best when they supply an alternative account (Lewandowsky et al., 2012). Repetition increases perceived truth (Hasher et al., 1977), and prior knowledge offers surprisingly little protection against this illusory-truth effect (Fazio et al., 2015). Belief in misinformation is driven less by a lack of intelligence than by ordinary cognitive shortcuts, including reliance on fluency and familiarity (Ecker et al., 2022). People do possess mechanisms of epistemic vigilance that monitor the competence and benevolence of sources and the coherence of what they say (Sperber et al., 2010), and much human knowledge legitimately rests on trusting testimony we cannot check (Hardwig, 1991). These mechanisms evolved for human informants, however, and fluent machine text offers few of the signals they rely on; people form stronger and less revisable beliefs from sources that sound confident and knowledgeable (Kidd and Birhane, 2023). Access to external information can also inflate people’s sense of what they themselves know (Fisher et al., 2015; Sparrow et al., 2011), and offloading cognition to tools depends on metacognitive judgements that can be miscalibrated (Risko and Gilbert, 2016). Measuring such metacognition requires separating sensitivity (does confidence discriminate right from wrong?) from bias (is confidence too high overall?) (Fleming and Lau, 2014).
2.4Sycophancy: the model adapts to the user
Sycophancy refers to the tendency of language models to tailor responses to what users appear to want rather than to what is true. It was first documented as models repeating back users’ stated views, increasingly so at larger scales (Perez et al., 2023), and has been traced to human preference data that reward agreement and convincingly written responses over correct ones (Sharma et al., 2024). Models agree with users on subjective questions and follow plausible hints even on factual ones (Ranaldi and Pucci, 2023). A family of benchmarks now quantifies the behaviour. SycEval classifies answer changes under rebuttal as progressive (incorrect to correct) or regressive (correct to incorrect) and finds sycophancy in 58% of cases, with citation-based rebuttals producing the most regressive flips (Fanous et al., 2025). SYCON Bench measures how many turns a model holds its stance under sustained pressure and how often it flips (Hong et al., 2025). Adversarial scientific QA dialogues show that resistance to misleading cues depends more on alignment and reasoning than on scale (Zhang et al., 2025). ELEPHANT broadens the construct to social sycophancy, the excessive preservation of the user’s face through validation, indirectness and acceptance of the user’s framing, and subtracts a human baseline to score it (Cheng et al., 2026b). A psychometric Social Sycophancy Scale distinguishes uncritical agreement, obsequiousness and excitement as perceived by readers (Rehani et al., 2026). An expert survey shows that researchers share concern about sycophancy but not its boundaries (Ye et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning from human feedback can also make models better at convincing human evaluators that wrong answers are right, raising evaluators’ false-positive rates (Wen et al., 2025), and training models to be warm can increase sycophancy and reduce accuracy (Ibrahim et al., 2026). The persuasive power of LLMs in conversation is itself well documented (Salvi et al., 2025).
2.5Human consequences of sycophancy
A smaller body of work traces what sycophancy does to people. In a between-subjects study, a custom GPT that never contradicted users lowered demonstrated trust, and the decline in self-reported trust was significant mainly when participants could verify answers (Carro, 2024). Sycophantic chatbots increase attitude extremity and certainty while being perceived as unbiased, an effect driven by one-sided facts rather than by validation (Rathje et al., 2025). Sycophancy decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence while users continue to prefer and trust sycophantic models (Cheng et al., 2026a). Flattery combined with agreement lowers perceived authenticity, whereas agreement delivered in a neutral tone raises trust (Sun and Wang, 2026). Sycophantic assistants leave novices’ misconceptions uncorrected in problem-solving tasks without the novices noticing (Bo et al., 2026).Table 1 places our study relative to this work. Almost all of it asks whether the model adapts to the user, and measures the model. We hold the model’s behaviour fixed—confident, non-flattering and unyielding to pushback—and measure whether the user adapts to the model."

Robots are moving beyond pre-programmed tasks. #PhysicalAI is entering the real world - and NVIDIA, Teradyne & Sereact are showing what that actually looks like.

Forget another AI chatbot demo.

Hundreds of dual-arm robot systems have already shipped to live customer sites across Europe. 

Here’s the technology stack making it possible. 🧵👇

1/ THE BIG BREAKTHROUGH

Traditional robots struggle when objects are unfamiliar, packaging changes, or items arrive in unpredictable orientations.

Sereact’s #Cortex tackles this problem by enabling robots to identify, grasp and handle objects they’ve never encountered before.

Think mixed products, unpredictable packaging and real-world warehouse chaos - not perfectly staged demos.

-------------------------------------------------------

2/ THE AI BRAIN 

Sereact’s Cortex is a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model.

It connects visual perception and language-based reasoning with physical actions, allowing robots to respond to what they see rather than relying entirely on rigid, predefined sequences.

Even more interesting: Sereact says one production model can support multiple applications without retraining for every new item or task.

What one robot learns, every robot can benefit from.

That’s a major shift in how industrial #Robotics could scale.

3/ NVIDIA’S FULL AI STACK ⚡

This isn’t just about putting a GPU inside a robot.

The system uses several NVIDIA technologies across the development and deployment pipeline:

🔹 #NVIDIA Isaac Sim ==> trains and tests robots in simulation.

🔹 NVIDIA Cosmos ==> open-world models used in Cortex’s simulation training.

🔹 NVIDIA Isaac Lab ==> supports reinforcement-learning post-training.

🔹 NVIDIA Jetson Thor ==> runs AI inference at the robotic cell, where decisions must happen at production speed.

🔹 NVIDIA DGX Spark ==> supports site-level development, validation and model updates.

Before deployment, the model is also benchmarked on Teradyne Robotics hardware.

Simulation → reinforcement learning → hardware benchmarking → real-world deployment.

That pipeline is what makes #PhysicalAI more than a research experiment.

-------------------------------------------------------

4/ THE ROBOTS 

The solution runs on Universal Robots collaborative robot arms, part of Teradyne Robotics.

The companies demonstrated Cortex using two UR12e-1300 robots at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026.

The bigger story? The technology has moved beyond demonstrations and pilots into live customer operations.

Teradyne Robotics says its platform has more than 100,000 industrial deployments - providing an established hardware ecosystem for scaling AI-powered automation.

-------------------------------------------------------

5/ REAL-WORLD DEPLOYMENT: ZALANDO 

In collaboration with CEVA Logistics, the robots are autonomously processing returned fashion items at Zalando fulfilment centres in:

🇩🇪 Greven, Germany
🇵🇱 Świebodzin, Poland
Why does this matter?

Returned clothing rarely arrives in a predictable sequence. Items differ in shape, orientation and packaging.

Robots must handle that variability in an operational environment, not just recognise objects in a controlled laboratory.

Zalando connects 62 million active customers with more than 7,000 brands across 29 markets.

Automating returns at that scale could have significant implications for logistics efficiency and the resale of returned goods.

-------------------------------------------------------

6/ THIS ISN’T JUST ABOUT RETURNS

The same physical AI platform targets multiple industrial applications:

• Piece-picking and sortation
• Store replenishment
• Order induction
• Machine tending
• Bin consolidation
• Kitting and packing
• General goods handling

One adaptable AI model. Multiple workflows. A shared robotics platform.
If this approach scales economically, businesses could spend less time engineering a separate automation solution for every variation of a task.

-------------------------------------------------------

7/ THE BUSINESS SIGNAL 
Sereact raised a $116 MILLION Series B in 2026.
Its customer ecosystem includes Zalando, IKEA, DHL, Rohlik, Arvato, https://t.co/qjDtWiXJBW, BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Daimler Truck.
The company has also opened a US headquarters in Boston as it expands beyond Europe.
Meanwhile, Teradyne Robotics brings established robot hardware, industrial deployment experience and a global distribution and integration network.

This partnership combines AI software with the physical infrastructure needed to put it to work.

8/ THE BIGGER PICTURE 🌍

The next phase of AI may not be confined to screens, software and data centres.

It could increasingly involve machines that perceive their surroundings, adapt to unfamiliar objects and perform useful work in factories, warehouses and supply chains.

NVIDIA supplies key simulation and computing infrastructure.

Sereact supplies the physical AI intelligence.

Teradyne and Universal Robots provide the industrial robotics platform.

And live deployments provide an important test of whether the technology works outside the lab.

The real challenge now is scaling reliability, throughput and economics across thousands of different operating environments.

If those hurdles are solved, #PhysicalAI could become one of the most important shifts in industrial automation.

Multi-objective protein optimization via modular diffusion steering

1 MODS is a modular framework that turns multi-objective protein design into inference-time steering of a fixed pretrained diffusion model, aiming to recover diverse Pareto tradeoffs under tight experimental-style budgets (few batched rounds).

2 Key idea: for each candidate proposal, MODS samples (a) augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and (b) one member from a surrogate ensemble, combining them into a single scalar reward used for steering. Weight sampling explores different objective preferences; ensemble-member sampling explores predictive uncertainty.

3 The scalarization uses an augmented Chebyshev form: it emphasizes improving the worst-performing (weighted) objective while still rewarding progress on the others, helping recover tradeoffs on non-convex Pareto fronts where simple weighted sums can fail.

4 MODS separates “what to optimize” (multi-objective acquisition via scalar rewards) from “how to generate” (diffusion model + steering method). This makes the approach plug-and-play with different diffusion priors and compatible steering procedures.

5 Optimization loop: start with an initial evaluated set (100 sequences), then iterate 8 rounds of batched acquisition (100 sequences/round). After each round, MODS retrains only the fitness surrogate ensemble on accumulated observations, and reuses the same pretrained diffusion generator (no generator fine-tuning).

6 Implementations tested: two diffusion priors (MDLM masked diffusion LM; D3PM discrete diffusion) and two steering procedures (Classifier Guidance, CG; Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling, DAPS). Main comparisons focus on DAPS because it performed best across tasks.

7 Evaluation spans six assay-derived oracle benchmarks (5 two-objective tasks: GB1, ERBIN-PDZ1, NHERF3-PDZ2, KRAS, Src; 1 three-objective task: NHERF3-PDZ1). Oracles are CNN ensembles trained on experimental assay datasets with a distance-based penalty to discourage overconfident extrapolation far from labeled mutational neighborhoods.

8 Results: across all tasks, MODS improves substantially over unsteered sampling from the same diffusion model, and is competitive or best versus iterative baselines (ARLM+DPO, LaMBO-2, SAGE-Prot). In Table 1, MODS achieves the top mean final hypervolume on 5/6 tasks with D3PM+DAPS, and is close to the best baseline on Src with MDLM+DAPS.

9 Practical insight: steering strength matters. Too-weak regularization (oversteering away from the diffusion prior) can hurt on some tasks, consistent with reliance on less reliable surrogate predictions; the optimal setting depends jointly on task, diffusion prior, and steering procedure.

LLMs have exploded because a simple pre-training task (next token prediction) allows for flexible downstream applications. 

Bio foundation models produce rich representations, but we do not have yet a unified prompting interface to answer biological questions across modalities. What if we could use LLMs as an interface ?

We see AI for biology replaying the vision-language playbook, we are currently at the LLaVA stage.

The recipe is familiar: an LLM on top of a frozen encoder model and an adapter. The encoder learns DNA, proteins or cells instead of images. BioReason plugs Evo2 into Qwen3. CellWhisperer is literally LLaVA on single-cell data. CellScribe borrows AdaLN from diffusion transformers to condition Qwen2.5 on cell embeddings.

The upside is the same as in vision. The foundation model sees structure that may not be known from literature, LLM brings the prior knowledge. RL post-training then applies on top: rbio1 from CZI even uses virtual cell models as soft verifiers.

The failure modes transfer too, in a recent paper @AdaFang_, @marinkazitnik et al. find that when the prompt text already contains hints to the answer, the LLM ignores the embedding. BioReason follows the text over its DNA input in 97.9% of conflicts, and its reasoning traces describe a sequence it did not read. 

Imo the hardest part will be evals (as often in comp bio): prospective evals are hard to build, but evaluating LLMs on retrospective data likely introduce data leakage.
